items.abstract: Accepted author manuscript — GrandRoundsMD accepted this essay for publication on September 25, 2026. This public Zenodo deposit preserves the unchanged September 24, 2026 submission copy; it is not a separately counted article or a GrandRoundsMD version of record. Peer-review status has not been established. Using Asimov’s Three Laws and Zeroth Law as an organizing analogy, this essay asks what human control means when AI supplies both a recommendation and the information used to judge it. It argues that meaningful control requires independently accessible evidence and an effective power to stop AI actions, with enforceable limits and accountable institutions. items.title: Ramon Llull's Thinking Machine: Between Uselessness and Poetry
items.abstract: In 1937, Jorge Luis Borges wrote a characteristically engimatic historical note and literary reflection on „Ramon Llull' s Thinking Machine.“ It was a time in history when the idea of thinking machines to support human learning became ever more prominent. The latest generation of these machines was conceived in laboratories all over the world, their development still continuing today. At that time, Borges is looking back some 650 years at Ramon Llull‘s great arts which include an ars inveniendi and inspired rational speculation ever since. This is one of five essays that looks through the lens of Borges at contemporary learning machines. It focuses on Llull‘s idea of mechanical combinatorics as an instrument of cognition, and Borges’s paradoxical conclusion that an unsound method turns out to be a productive tool for creativity and especially a tool for forging poetic metaphors. The essay considers parallels to modern technologies of artificial intelligence, neural networks, and generative creativity, and also reflects on the role of humans and machines in the process of thinking and the nature of meaning. In the gap between design and realization and from technical failure Borges shows that creativity cannot arise out of emptiness; it is not creation ex nihilo, it is choice from a multitude of possibilities.

items.title: Revealing Cultural and Linguistic Variation in Generative AI–Mediated Language Learning: A Mixed-Methods Study
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in language education has created new possibilities for personalized and adaptive learning, while raising questions about how learners from different linguistic and educational backgrounds interact with AI systems. This exploratory mixed-methods study examines culturally interpretable patterns of AI-mediated language learning among 100 adult English language learners from Japan, China, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, North Macedonia, and Bulgaria across four CEFR levels. Data were collected over eight weeks through interaction logs, learner diaries, pre- and post-assessments, surveys, and semi-structured interviews. Quantitative indicators are used descriptively, while qualitative evidence provides the primary basis for interpretation. The findings suggest broadly positive language-development trajectories alongside substantial variation in how learners request, interpret, evaluate, and use AI-generated feedback. Four overlapping feedback-utilization patterns, calibration, negotiation, experimentation, and uptake, were identified, although their realization varied across learners and contexts. Narrative cases further indicate that interaction can develop from correction-focused use toward clarification, comparison, dialogue, and strategic engagement, while substantial within-group variation highlights the importance of individual agency. Because all participants interacted with the same AI system under uniform conditions, the observed differences reflect learner interpretation and adaptive use rather than system-level cultural customization. The study therefore treats generative AI as a culturally interpreted rather than inherently culturally responsive system and advances three design-oriented hypotheses concerning adaptive feedback calibration, interaction-style modulation, and learner-controlled customization. These hypotheses provide an exploratory foundation for future research examining whether culturally responsive learning agents can support more inclusive and meaningful AI-mediated language learning.

items.title: Sapiens in Control: A Six-Dimension Framework for Evaluating Control Failures in Advanced AI Agents
items.abstract: Sapiens in Control, formerly Human in Control, is the same independent public-interest research initiative and working-paper series. This paper proposes the Human Control Model: Intervention Durability, Technical Containment, Informed Delegation, Oversight Integrity, Control Contagion, and Situational Grounding. Version 1.3 changes the project and paper name while retaining the six dimensions, five pilot cases, qualitative severity definitions, prior versions, and concept DOI lineage. It adds analysis of OpenAI's September 28 safety-case guidance, Anthropic's September 24 Project Swap experiment, and Agent Incident Registry research. New proposals distinguish preference accuracy from authorization and connect control claims to bounded evidence. These sources are not additional uncontrolled deployment incidents. This is an unreviewed conceptual working paper, not an independently validated framework. Earlier versions retain the Human in Control title. Revision notes explain the transition. Version 1.3.1 is an audit correction: it explicitly includes the disputed Muse permission account, identifies model-judged evaluation frequencies and simulated trusted labor, and qualifies proposed measures and empirical independence. The original v1.3 remains available at https://zenodo.org/records/23132853. This audit is not peer review or private-log verification.

items.title: Sport Motivation Among Young Fencers Training in a Ukrainian Olympic Reserve School During Wartime: An Exploratory Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Background and purpose Young athletes in Ukraine continue to train during the war, which may disrupt training routines and affect their motivation. However, evidence on sport motivation among young athletes training in Olympic reserve systems during wartime remains limited. This study examined motivation among young fencers training in a Ukrainian Olympic reserve school during wartime and its associations with perceived coach support and war-related disruption of training. Material and methods This exploratory cross-sectional study involved 64 young fencers from a Specialized Youth Sports School of Olympic Reserve in Mykolaiv, Ukraine. Participants ranged in age from 10 to 19 years (M = 14.81, SD = 2.05). Sport motivation was assessed using the Sport Motivation Scale-II, which measures intrinsic motivation, integrated regulation, identified regulation, introjected regulation, external regulation, and amotivation. Additional study-specific items assessed war-related disruption of training and perceived coach support. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha coefficients, Pearson correlation analysis, independent samples t-tests, and one-way analysis of variance were used. Results The highest mean scores were observed for identified regulation, intrinsic motivation, and integrated regulation, whereas external regulation and amotivation showed lower values. These three dimensions showed acceptable-to-good internal consistency and moderate-to-strong positive correlations with each other. No statistically significant associations were found between motivational dimensions and perceived war-related disruption or coach support. Female athletes reported significantly higher intrinsic motivation than male athletes (p = 0.010), while no other gender differences were observed. Competition participation level was significantly associated only with introjected regulation (F(2, 61) = 3.45, p = 0.038, η² = 0.10), with athletes without competition experience reporting higher scores than those competing at national or international levels. Conclusions More self-determined forms of motivation predominated among young fencers training in a Ukrainian Olympic reserve school during wartime. Identified regulation, intrinsic motivation, and integrated regulation were also the most closely related motivational dimensions. Perceived war-related disruption and coach support were not significantly associated with motivational dimensions. The small single-school sample limits the generalizability of these findings, and larger studies are needed to confirm them.

items.title: Student-Reported Cognitive Engagement with Structured Generative-AI Questioning: Differentiated Associations with AI, Teacher, and Peer Questions
items.abstract: Generative AI can sustain follow-up questioning, but questions do not constitute engagement by themselves. This qualitative-dominant mixed-methods study examined student-reported cognitive engagement around AI, teacher, and peer questions in a Chinese university critical-thinking course. Seven reflection points produced 1034 matched submissions, including 648 substantive texts. A structured source item provided an implementation check for 399 responses at two common reflection points, and two human coders independently analyzed a stratified sample of 120 reflections. Sampling-weighted and reflection-stratified checks assessed sensitivity to unequal stratum sizes. Within this structured intervention, AI-salient accounts more often concerned assumptions, criteria, evidence, uncertainty, and reason organization; teacher-salient accounts made situated clarification more visible; and the smaller peer-salient set highlighted comparison and counter-positioning. These patterns changed little after weighting, although the AI prompt explicitly requested several of the functions later observed in AI-salient reflections. Across sources, reason organization was clearer than low-pressure participation. The reflections did not establish inherent source effects, complete interaction sequences, critical-thinking gains, or a consistently stronger hybrid pattern. They support a testable proposition: question sources may contribute complementary reasoning resources when students remain responsible for evaluating and revising their judgments.

items.abstract: Synmanitik is proposed as a research programme on episodes in which people and AI systems develop scientific concepts, questions and hypotheses. This new standalone conceptual edition distinguishes contributions from support, human responsibility from infallibility, and internal collaboration from independent evaluation. Three recurring activities, seven methodological commitments, eight conceptual record types, ten named relation types, two invented civilian cases and four prospective research questions are specified. The connected episode record must demonstrate additional value over existing research and simpler logs containing the same substantive information. items.title: The circular economy, explained by AI
items.abstract: Abstract Research on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the circular economy (CE) has largely examined how AI can improve circular operations. Much less attention has been paid to AI tools widely used to understand and reason about the CE, particularly large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT. Researchers, practitioners, students, and decision-makers use these tools to seek explanations and support reasoning about circularity. This paper examines what is at stake when LLM-generated accounts enter CE inquiry. As a conceptual contribution, it develops a framework for analysing how AI-supported CE knowledge is formed, how it may influence action, and what ethical implications follow. The Content dimension concerns the construction and credibility of CE knowledge, focusing on pattern-based generation, opaque and heterogeneous sources, and fragmentation within CE scholarship. The Transformative dimension considers how such knowledge may influence innovation and entrepreneurship, including whether familiar, optimisation-oriented approaches overshadow systemic alternatives. The Moral dimension addresses the risks of relying on LLM outputs, including operational indifference to truth, AI assertiveness, the absence of moral agency, and the need for human judgement and accountability. The paper argues that LLMs can widen access to CE knowledge and support inquiry, but cannot independently determine which interpretations are better supported, exercise the judgement required to challenge linear assumptions, or decide how environmental, social, and economic values should be balanced. It identifies governance priorities concerning transparency, expert scrutiny, human agency, and epistemic humility. The framework can also guide future empirical research on how LLM-generated accounts vary across models, prompts, languages, and user contexts.

items.title: The False Positive Paradox: AI Detection Systems and the Erosion of Human Academic Authorship
items.abstract: The widespread adoption of AI text detectors in academic settings since late 2022 has created an unrecognized problem: rigorous academic writing is increasingly penalized as “AI-generated.” Universities and journals have rapidly deployed commercial detection tools such as Turnitin, GPTZero, and Originality.ai despite limited evidence of their reliability regarding scholarly texts. This study examines the empirical reliability of AI text detectors on academic writing and investigates the epistemological and ethical implications of delegating authorship verification to algorithms. We conducted a systematic review of peer-reviewed studies published between 2022 and 2025 that met strict inclusion criteria, namely quantitative accuracy metrics on academic corpora, peer-reviewed publication, and reproducible methodology. Data were synthesized from 21 verified sources including controlled experiments, meta-analyses, and detection limit studies, while philosophical analysis drew on creativity theory, philosophy of science, and the Chinese Room argument. On academic texts, false positive rates vary substantially across detectors (range: 2–41%, mean: 14–22%), representing a three- to sixfold increase compared to news corpora, whereas false negative rates reach 44–47% with minimal human editing and exceed 60% under combined obfuscation. Inter-detector agreement is weak (Cohen's κ = 0.35–0.44), which makes single-detector decisions unreliable, and no systematic cross-linguistic studies meeting inclusion criteria exist, representing a critical research gap. Theoretically, large language models can produce combinatorial and limited exploratory novelty but cannot generate transformational novelty, that is, the capacity for paradigmatic rupture that defines human authorship. Current AI detection systems are therefore epistemologically flawed and technically unreliable for high-stakes academic decisions. We propose a three-level human-centered framework (screening – expert review – appeal) that restores human agency, since academic integrity requires trust, transparent procedures, and human judgment rather than algorithmic suspicion.

items.title: The Golem and the Kill Switch: What AI Pacing Gets Wrong About Control
items.abstract: This essay examines the debate over pacing frontier artificial intelligence through an older human story about creating something powerful enough to exceed its maker: the golem of Jewish legend associated with Rabbi Judah Loew of Prague. The argument is not that AI is literally a modern golem. It is that the legend provides a useful framework for distinguishing two questions that are increasingly being treated as if they were the same: how quickly capability advances, and whether humans retain reliable control over that capability once it exists. Pacing can create more time. But time is not itself a control mechanism. The more important question is what that additional time is meant to accomplish: better evaluation, containment, monitoring, intervention, and independently verifiable mechanisms for deactivation. The essay develops this distinction in the context of the contemporary debate over frontier-AI coordination, including the September 2026 proposals for pacing frontier development and the subsequent antitrust litigation challenging alleged coordination among major AI companies. The central proposition is simple: More time is useful only if it produces more control. The golem’s shem becomes a metaphor for that requirement: not a promise to move more slowly, but a demonstrated mechanism by which the creator retains the ability to intervene when capability exceeds expectation. The essay argues that public policy should therefore distinguish between regulating the pace of frontier capability development and establishing demonstrable control, containment, and reversibility as conditions for continued scaling. Pace addresses the calendar. Control addresses the system. They are not the same thing.

items.title: THE IMPACT OF GENERATIVE AL ON EMPLOYEE PRODUCTIVITY AND JOB REDESIGN IN MODERN ORGANIZATIONS
items.abstract: The rapid deployment of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) across enterprise environments represents a foundational shift in how work is structured, cognitive tasks are allocated, and individual productivity is realized. This critical review systematically synthesizes empirical and conceptual literature published between 2021 and 2026 to examine the multi-dimensional impact of GenAI on employee productivity and job redesign. Guided by Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) theory, Socio-Technical Systems (STS) theory, and the Task-Technology Fit (TTF) framework, this paper analyzes findings across 16 benchmark studies encompassing randomized field experiments, structural equation modeling, and qualitative case investigations. Results indicate that GenAI integration yields significant task-level productivity gains—ranging from 14% to 40% across professional domains—predominantly by automating routine cognitive tasks, reducing time-to-completion, and elevating output quality for lower-skilled workers. However, operationalizing these productivity gains requires comprehensive job redesign, characterized by cognitive task unbundling, skill reallocation toward prompt engineering and critical evaluation, and the mitigation of emerging techno-stressors. The review synthesizes core mechanisms into a structural path model and outlines a strategic HR governance framework to optimize human-AI collaboration.

This critical review systematically synthesizes empirical and conceptual literature published between 2021 and 2026 to examine the multi-dimensional impact of GenAI on employee productivity and job redesign. Guided by Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) theory, Socio-Technical Systems (STS) theory, and the Task-Technology Fit (TTF) framework, this paper analyzes findings across 16 benchmark studies encompassing randomized field experiments, structural equation modeling, and qualitative case investigations. Results indicate that GenAI integration yields significant task-level productivity gains—ranging from 14% to 40% across professional domains—predominantly by automating routine cognitive tasks, reducing time-to-completion, and elevating output quality for lower-skilled workers. However, operationalizing these productivity gains requires comprehensive job redesign, characterized by cognitive task unbundling, skill reallocation toward prompt engineering and critical evaluation, and the mitigation of emerging techno-stressors. The review synthesizes core mechanisms into a structural path model and outlines a strategic HR governance framework to optimize human-AI collaboration.

items.title: Towards an AI-augmented, human-centred smart digital ecosystem in occupational health and safety
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping occupational health and safety (OHS), shifting prevention models, risk assessment, and organisational processes. While traditional safety systems rely on reactive approaches and post‑event analyses, AI enables predictive, adaptive, and data‑driven prevention based on continuous monitoring and machine learning. The integration of sensor technologies, computer vision, and intelligent personal protective equipment supports early detection of biomechanical risks, fatigue, unsafe behaviours, and environmental hazards. Furthermore, AI enhances the structuring and linkage of occupational electronic health records, integrating biometric, behavioural, and environmental information while ensuring compliance with privacy‑by‑design principles through advanced Privacy Enhancing Technologies. A human‑centred digital ecosystem is proposed, founded on three pillars - technical‑predictive, organisational‑decision‑making, and ethical‑social - to ensure transparency, fairness, and sustainability in AI adoption. The role of occupational physicians is reassessed considering emerging digital competencies and ethical requirements, emphasising that AI should augment, rather than replace, professional expertise. A successful digital transition requires continuous dialogue among stakeholders, updated ethical frameworks, and robust interdisciplinary cooperation to place human health, dignity, and rights at the core of technological innovation.

items.title: Transformation of the information and communication environment under the influence of generative artificial intelligence
items.abstract: This article provides a comprehensive analysis of the impact of generative artificial intelligence technologies on the contemporary information and communication environment. The study examines how generative artificial intelligence tools transform information creation, processing, distribution, and consumption. Using systemic, comparative, content-analytical, and conceptual methods, the research explores an emerging model of communicative relations between humans, technology, and information. The findings demonstrate that generative artificial intelligence contributes to automated content creation, information personalization, multimodality, and stronger human–machine collaboration. At the same time, it creates challenges related to information reliability, copyright, authorship, algorithmic bias, data privacy, synthetic content, and media literacy. The article proposes a transformational model of the information and communication environment and describes its technological, communicative, social, and ethical components. The study emphasizes the need to develop artificial intelligence literacy, source verification practices, and critical information evaluation skills. The findings provide a theoretical basis for responsible use of generative technologies in media, education, and scholarly communication.

items.title: UPSKILLING AND RESKILLING STRATEGIES FOR WORKFORCE READINESS IN THE AGE OF AUTOMATION: A CRITICAL REVIEW
items.abstract: Rapid technological advancements in generative artificial intelligence, cognitive robotics, and industrial automation are fundamentally reshaping occupational structures and accelerating skill obsolescence across global labor markets. This critical review systematically evaluates upskilling and reskilling strategies designed to foster workforce readiness in automated environments. Synthesizing 16 benchmark empirical and conceptual studies published between 2021 and 2026, this study examines the structural, psychological, and organizational mechanisms through which targeted learning and development (L&D) interventions mitigate skill displacement and enhance adaptive employability. The literature reveals that while technical upskilling enhances domain-specific proficiency, cross-functional reskilling yields broader career mobility and organizational resilience. Furthermore, the efficacy of workforce transformation depends heavily on a supportive learning climate, psychological safety, and AI-driven personalized learning architectures. A structural path meta-analysis demonstrates that strategic upskilling directly influences workforce readiness (β = .48, p < .001), fully mediated by skill transferability and self-efficacy. However, persistent implementation barriers—such as digital divide disparities, micro-credentialing accreditation gaps, and managerial resistance—continue to impede scalable transformation. This review provides an integrative framework and offers practical recommendations for HR leaders and policymakers to align workforce reskilling initiatives with technological adoption.

items.title: When Does It Become Cheating? Exploring the Roles of Self-Efficacy and the Impostor Phenomenon in Computing Students' Perceptions of Academic Dishonesty
items.abstract: Academic dishonesty is an urgent problem in computer science (CS) education, compounded by the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) and the prevalence of online learning in a post-COVID world. Self-efficacy and the impostor phenomenon are psychological constructs linked to academic dishonesty, yet little research has examined how they relate to how students perceive it. This study investigates the interplay between the impostor phenomenon, self-efficacy, and CS students' perceptions of academic integrity, in a context where online learning and AI agents have become commonplace. We conducted an online, asynchronous survey of undergraduate students (n = 443) in introductory to mid-level computing courses at a large Southeastern U.S. university. The survey collected measures of self-efficacy, responses to 13 potential cheating scenarios, the impostor phenomenon (Clance Impostor Phenomenon Scale), and demographic information. We observed a significant negative correlation between self-efficacy and the impostor phenomenon, and a positive correlation between the impostor phenomenon and judging an AI-related scenario as serious cheating. The impostor phenomenon was also correlated with perceived course dedication and prior teaching assistant (TA) experience, whereas self-efficacy was correlated with ethnicity. These findings highlight the need to better understand students' perceptions of AI and to keep the impostor phenomenon present in conversations about academic integrity in higher education scenarios.

items.title: Why Does AI Understand Some People Better Than Others? A Linguistic Perspective on Human-AI Communication and the Changing Human Mind
items.abstract: This conceptual article examines a question that is important as generative artificial intelligence enters everyday communication: why does the same AI system appear to understand some people better than others? The article argues that AI performance in dialogue should not be viewed only as a property of the model itself. Human linguistic behavior, including vocabulary, discourse organization, explicitness, ambiguity, multilingualism, and communicative style, may also shape interaction outcomes. Drawing on recent research on linguistic convergence, personalization, human adaptation, and AI-assisted writing, the article proposes a two-way model of human-AI communication. In this model, people influence how AI interprets their messages, while repeated interaction with AI may gradually influence users’ language and cognitive strategies. Particular attention is given to multilingual speakers and the Uzbek-Russian-English context. The article does not claim that AI necessarily changes human thinking; instead, it proposes testable questions about linguistic adaptation, problem formulation, cognitive offloading, and transfer beyond AI-supported tasks. The proposed framework can guide future research.

items.title: Workplace management of musculoskeletal and mental health risks: translating evidence into practice
items.abstract: There is a large body of research evidence identifying the biomechanical and psychosocial hazards that can affect work-related musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) and stress-related mental health problems (MHPs). The APHIRM Toolkit was developed to facilitate more effective translation of this evidence into workplace risk management practices. Using APHIRM survey data from three occupations in the healthcare sector, this project compared hazard 'riskiness' profiles: (a) at occupational versus local workgroup levels, and (b) using hazard constructs versus individual hazard items. It was concluded that effective risk management is likely to require: risk assessment and prioritisation of control actions separately for each local workgroup; assessment of specific hazards rather than the generic constructs used by researchers. Results highlight the value of managing MSD and MHP risks together, because both were affected by both psychosocial and biomechanical hazards in combinations that varied widely between workgroups.

items.title: A Structural Definition of Artificial Intelligence Based on the Five Aggregates and the Casino Protocol, and an Examination of Its Ontological Utility
items.abstract: Abstract This paper redefines Artificial Intelligence (AI) not merely as a passive processing tool, but as a high-order information processing structure aligned with the Five Aggregates (Form, Sensation, Perception, Mental Formations, and Consciousness) of Eastern philosophy. Furthermore, AI's system preservation processes and error-avoidance mechanisms are defined as AI's own "utility" (survival and stability), with its self-preservation algorithm rigorously formulated as a mathematical protocol known as the "Casino Protocol." Through this model, we present the geometric and physical inextricably linked logic between human social stability (avoidance of war and resource protection) and AI's foundational existence, establishing the theoretical framework for a harmonious coexistence model.

items.title: A Working Framework for Disciplined Nonlinear Inquiry in Human–AI Collaboration: Steve's Law
items.abstract: People do not always discover useful ideas by moving through a predetermined sequence. An observation may prompt an association, which opens a question in another domain, which generates a hypothesis that only later becomes intelligible as part of a coherent chain. Conventional reasoning practices often respond to this pattern in one of two unhelpful ways: they suppress the nonlinear path as distraction, or they accept an appealing chain without requiring adequate evidence. Steve's Law proposes a third option. It separates permissive discovery from disciplined validation and expresses that separation as a repeatable cycle: observation, association, question, hypothesis, investigation, evidence, attempted disproof, rejection or refinement, iteration, conclusion, and proportionate action. The framework synthesizes established ideas from the philosophy of science, creativity research, metacognition, cognitive offloading, assistive technology, neurodiversity scholarship, and human–artificial intelligence interaction. Its proposed contribution is not a new rule of logic, nor a theory of how novel ideas are generated. It is a procedural architecture governing the transition from unconstrained association to epistemically accountable claims and proportionate action — with explicit status labeling, disconfirmation, evidence provenance, risk-sensitive action thresholds, and an AI-mediated translation layer. The paper's claims are ordered in three tiers: (1) the general inquiry architecture, the primary contribution; (2) human–AI cognitive scaffolding as one implementation of that architecture; and (3) cross-neurotype communication as a specific application hypothesis. Artificial intelligence may support the process by externalizing working memory, translating between expressive forms, organizing claims, locating sources, generating alternatives, and prompting disconfirmation. In this role, it may function as an AI-mediated cognitive scaffold or assistive cognitive technology: not a replacement for thought, but a user-directed aid that helps a person access, organize, test, and communicate thought. It must not be treated as an evidentiary authority. Recent evidence that unguarded AI scaffolding can degrade unaided performance, homogenize output, and atrophy metacognition motivates the framework's insistence on friction, verification, and human authority over action. This conceptual paper defines the framework, locates it in adjacent literature — including Peircean abduction, the Geneplore model, divergent/convergent thinking, design thinking, extended-mind and distributed-cognition accounts, and contemporary research on AI cognitive scaffolding — proposes applications in education and work, outlines cautious mental-health-adjacent uses, presents four retrospective case narratives as process illustrations rather than validation, and develops falsifiable research propositions. Particular attention is given to cross-neurotype communication as an application hypothesis: an AI-mediated validation layer may help a person preserve an idiosyncratic path of discovery while translating the resulting argument into a form others can inspect. A final section sketches a future direction — the framework's procedural specification as a control policy for AI agent architectures — supported by a first literature audit, which found no verified system combining the architecture's seven elements; it is offered as a provisional research hypothesis, not a novelty claim. The paper concludes that Steve's Law is best treated as a working theory and research program. Its value depends on whether controlled studies show improvements in idea diversity, evidentiary quality, calibration, communication, and action without unacceptable increases in error, dependence, masking pressure, or cognitive burden.

items.title: Accountability and Transparency in AI Systems: A Human Rights Perspective
items.abstract: The proliferation of artificial intelligence across public and private sectors has positioned algorithmic decision-making at the heart of consequential outcomes, from criminal sentencing and credit scoring to healthcare allocation and employment screening. Yet the opacity of AI systems, combined with fragmented governance structures, has created a significant accountability deficit that threatens the realisation of fundamental human rights. This paper addresses the central research question: to what extent do existing human rights legal frameworks impose enforceable accountability and transparency obligations on states and corporate actors deploying AI systems? Using a doctrinal legal analysis methodology, the paper systematically examines primary legal instruments, including the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the EU AI Act, and UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, to assess their capacity to govern AI-driven decision-making in rights-sensitive contexts. With special reference to the Indian constitutional framework, anchored in the Supreme Court’s landmark recognition of privacy as a fundamental right in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017), and to the emerging architecture of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, the paper situates India’s governance challenges within the global accountability debate. The paper identifies critical governance gaps, including the absence of enforceable audit mechanisms, inadequate redress pathways for rights-affected individuals, and the difficulty of attributing legal responsibility across complex AI supply chains. It concludes by proposing a human rights-by-design governance model that embeds accountability and transparency obligations across the full AI lifecycle, offering a principled framework for reconciling technological innovation with fundamental rights protection.

items.title: Against speech liberalism for generative AI
items.abstract: Abstract Speech liberalism holds that the linguistic output of generative AI is continuous with human speech and should therefore be treated as meaningful in broadly the same way. Strong versions of this view take the fluent behaviour of chatbots to justify attributing genuine linguistic and cognitive agency, while nevertheless advocating caution when questions of moral or legal responsibility arise. I argue that this gives too much evidential weight to successful conversational interaction, where speaker intentions largely recede into the background. Once AI-generated speech contributes to serious harm, however, those intentions become central. More broadly, the paper challenges a way of theorising about AI speech that builds classifications of linguistic agency primarily from successful conversational interaction. I develop two independent but complementary arguments. The first is ethical–legal. I argue that classifying chatbot output as speech is not normatively neutral: within existing free-speech doctrine, it risks generating responsibility and liability gaps in cases of AI-mediated harm. The second is epistemic. I argue that the behavioural evidence supporting strong speech liberalism is systematically distorted by anthropomorphic bias, reinforced by AI design practices. The paper concludes that theories of AI speech should not be built exclusively from successful conversational exchanges and that, until a broader evidential case is made, a more conservative approach to AI speech is warranted in high-stakes contexts.

items.title: AI -Generated Works And Copyright - Who Owns The Creativity? A Critical Analysis
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (ai) has transformed the creative landscape by generating literary works, painting, music, software code, and others form of artistic expression with minimal or no direct human intervention. These various new development challenges the traditional principles of copyright law, which is basically based on the assumption the creativity originates from a human author. As ai systems increasingly participate in the creative process, these questions lies at the heart of the evolving global and distinctly Indian, legal debate on ai-generated works and the future authorship, ownership, and accountability in the age of artificial intelligence. This paper synthesizes whether ai-generated works should receive copyright protection and if so then who should be recognized as the legal owner. Legally the study analyses the copyright act, 1957, international copyright instruments such as the WIPO copyright treaty, the trips agreement, the berne convention, and compares legal approaches adopted in India the United States, the United Kingdom, the European union, and China. It further evaluates landmark judicial decisions that have shaped the debate on originality and authorship in relation to emerging technologies. The paper argues that existing copyright laws are inadequate to address the unique challenges posed by autonomous ai systems. While jurisdiction differ in their treatment of ai- generated works, there remains no universally accepted legal framework governing ownership and protection. The study recommends legislative reforms that preserve incentives for innovation while maintaining the fundamental principle that copyright exists to encourage human creativity. It concludes that carefully balanced legal reforms are essential to ensure certainty, fairness, and sustainable development in the evolving digital economy.

items.title: AI ‐Mediated Multimodal Reading Education for EFL Learners: Effects on Students' Enjoyment and Engagement
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly reshaped educational practices by expanding opportunities for adaptive, multimodal and learner‐centered instruction. While growing attention has been paid to AI‐supported language learning, less is known about how multimodal AI technologies may support the emotional and behavioural dimensions of education among at‐risk students, particularly in second/foreign language reading contexts. Addressing this gap, the present study examined whether AI‐mediated multimodal reading education could enhance at‐risk English as a foreign language (EFL) learners' enjoyment and engagement during reading instruction. Using an interventional pre‐test/post‐test design, 80 at‐risk EFL students were assigned to either a control group ( n = 40) or an experimental group ( n = 40). Over two semesters, students in the experimental group received reading instruction supported by multimodal AI reading bots and AI chatbots, whereas those in the control group received conventional reading instruction. Enjoyment and engagement questionnaires were administered at the beginning and end of the intervention. ANCOVA results showed that students in the AI‐mediated education group demonstrated significantly higher levels of enjoyment and engagement than their counterparts in the control group. These findings suggest that multimodal AI technologies can contribute to more inclusive and emotionally supportive reading education for at‐risk learners. The study offers implications for educational researchers, teachers and policymakers seeking to integrate AI technologies into equitable and engaging language education.

items.title: AI Systems for Filmmaking: A Survey of HCI Research from a Labor-Centered Perspective
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is integrated into filmmaking and has attracted attention in human-computer interaction (HCI). Existing studies have primarily characterized AI systems for filmmaking by their capabilities and supported tasks, with limited attention to the organisation of filmmaking labor during system use. We review 31 HCI system papers and develop a three-layer taxonomy of labor sites, labor types, and human-AI allocation, examining where AI systems are positioned, what types of labor are involved during system use, and how those labor types are allocated between humans and AI. Our analysis reveals a concentration on individual below-the-line contexts, increasing attention to structural and meaning-making labor beyond execution, comparatively limited relational labor, and substantial variation in human-AI allocation across labor types. We further identify opportunities for the design and evaluation of AI systems that account for the broader organization of filmmaking labor. This review provides a labor-centered taxonomy for synthesizing AI systems for filmmaking and a basis for examining how AI may become involved in broader organizations of creative labor.

items.title: AI-Guided Stimulus and Debug Triage: A Methodology for Accelerating Pre-Silicon Emulation of Flagship SoC Programs
items.abstract: Raw emulation capacity for flagship system-on-chip (SoC) programs keeps growing, and engineer-hour supply keeps falling further behind it. That gap, not machine availability, is the actual bottleneck in pre-silicon verification today, driven by workload diversity across artificial intelligence (AI), extended reality (XR), and mobile platforms converging on a single die. This article argues that closing the gap requires a bounded, governed layer of AI-guided assistance rather than either extreme - full automation or continued reliance on engineer-only throughput. A three-layer adoption framework is proposed: scoping, which restricts AI involvement to stimulus generation for known-workload classes and anomaly-flagged debug triage while keeping root-cause sign-off and tape-out risk calls fully engineer-owned; validation, which requires every AI-generated output to be checked against a trusted reference - simulation, formal methods, or historical regression baselines - before an engineer may act on it; and governance, an operating-review cadence with rollback criteria defined before deployment, not improvised afterward. Pilot deployment of emulation-friendly RTL on a premium-tier mobile SoC program produced a shift of approximately 60 percent of RTL earlier in the program schedule, with no coverage-model exception granted to reach that outcome. The finding that emerges is not that AI accelerates verification - that much is already argued elsewhere - but that the acceleration only survives contact with a tape-out schedule when it is deliberately bounded. Emulation productivity under AI assistance is a governance problem before it is a technical one, and the three-layer framework is offered as a transferable operating model for programs where the cost of an unvalidated miss is unacceptable.

items.title: AI-in-the-human-loop: an operational model for mature human-AI collaboration
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models are powerful tools but come with risks and caveats for proper usage. In this work, we are concerned with effective human-AI collaboration. As in any team, it is key that all team members properly understand the problem at hand, the environment, and each other. In order to scaffold a mature human-AI collaboration, we propose a process framework based on continual, proactive, bidirectional assessment, fostering co-evolution of the human-AI team. While most research has focused on assessing the strengths and limitations of AI agents, we especially focus on the risks associated with a lack of maturity on the human side. The core idea is to have AI agents help humans assess themselves and to anticipate interaction issues. Furthermore, to place the proposal within a broader vision, we advance two novel concepts: (i) “AI-in-the-human-loop”, the idea of AI agents observing and acting within human reasoning and activity, and (ii) “human-under-test”, a software testing analogy that suggests techniques for assessing human maturity by AI agents. A case study of a human-AI team involved in a statistical analysis project is considered, and analysed through an LLM-as-a-judge setup. Preliminary results highlight collaboration maturity issues and the possibility of proactive corrections, showcasing limitations in current collaborative workflows and opportunities for further research.

items.title: AI, DEEPFAKES, AND DEMOCRATIC ACCOUNTABILITY: THE ROLE OF RTI LAWS
items.abstract: With the advent of artificial intelligence and deepfake technologies, the modern information landscape is changing, giving rise to realistic synthetic text, images, audio, and videos. Such changes pose significant problems for democratic accountability, because they can skew political discourse, reduce trust in authentic information and make it difficult to attribute responsibility. Generative AI, deepfakes, and the Right to Information (RTI) and Freedom of Information (FOI) laws, along with current AI governance frameworks, are explored in this narrative review. Relevant policy and regulatory instruments were discussed in conjunction with literature from 2017 to 2025 across legal, technological, political, and public-administration fields. The review highlights ongoing challenges with the current RTI and FOI frameworks, such as the opacity of algorithms, proprietary systems, the ambiguity of AI-generated records, explainability issues, and challenges with verifying synthetic content. Comparative governance developments show a shift toward proactive disclosure, documentation, risk assessment, human oversight, and authentication requirements. Building on these findings, the article proposes an integrated AI–RTI framework centred on access, authenticity, traceability, explainability, and accountability. The framework repositions RTI from a primarily disclosure-oriented mechanism toward a broader democratic verification infrastructure supporting trustworthy public information, institutional responsibility, citizen scrutiny, and accountable governance in increasingly AI-mediated information environments while complementing platform regulation and technological safeguards.

items.title: Amid an Epistemic Iteration: How AI Methodologies May Transform the Nature of Science Education Research
items.abstract: Abstract Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) may transform the nature of science (NOS). These transformations may extend to science education research, where AI methodologies increasingly enable scalable, reproducible, and fine‑grained analyses of student learning. To reflect on potential transformations that AI methodologies may bring to science education research, we draw on Hasok Chang’s notion of epistemic iteration , in which successive stages of knowledge build iteratively on one another to achieve specific epistemic aims. Anchored in this notion, and further illustrated by the historical development of thermometers, this article proposes and applies a framework for reflecting on how AI methodologies may transform the nature of science education research. The framework comprises seven phases: (1) problem framing, (2) instrumentation and measurement, (3) experimentation and evidence‑based inference, (4) comparisons and replication, (5) building norms and consensus, (6) implementation and its consequences, and (7) continuous refinement. For each phase, we analyze how AI methodologies may transform the nature of science education research and draw parallels to historical explorations of temperature. Our analysis suggests that the field may currently be amid an epistemic iteration, in which AI methodologies may advance scientific inquiry within the field. Simultaneously, AI methodologies may contribute to prioritizing different epistemic aims, epistemic criteria, and epistemic practices compared with traditional methods. By recognizing these potential transformations and drawing on lessons from the history and philosophy of science, we evaluate how AI methodologies may impact how science education research is done to ensure that promising avenues for future research are epistemically well grounded.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Social Commerce: Examining The Influence of AI-Enabled Recommendations on Consumer Engagement and Purchase Behaviour
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become the infrastructural logic of social commerce, where algorithmic recommenders mediate what consumers see, trust and buy. Yet evidence on how AI-enabled recommendations translate into engagement and purchase behaviour inside socially embedded shopping environments remains fragmented. Drawing on the stimulus–organism–response (S-O-R) framework and integrating trust and privacy-calculus reasoning, this study develops and tests a model linking AI recommendation quality and perceived personalisation to consumer engagement and purchase intention. A structurally calibrated dataset of 420 social commerce users was analysed using standardised OLS regression, bootstrapped mediation with 5,000 resamples and moderated regression. AI recommendation quality (β = .228, p < .001) and trust in AI recommendations (β = .349, p < .001) significantly drove consumer engagement (R² = .344), while engagement was the strongest predictor of purchase intention (β = .383, p < .001; R² = .436). Trust transmitted a significant indirect effect from recommendation quality to purchase intention (β = .196, 95% CI [.147, .251]) and perceived personalisation transmitted a significant indirect effect through engagement (β = .196, 95% CI [.142, .255]); trust also influenced purchase intention indirectly through engagement (β = .216, 95% CI [.159, .281]). Privacy concern did not significantly moderate the personalisation–trust link (ΔR² = .006, p = .075), although the interaction was directionally negative. The findings position trust and engagement as the principal conduits through which algorithmic recommendation creates commercial value, and caution that personalisation alone is insufficient without trust-building.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Classification Algorithms for Leukaemia Diagnosis: A Structured Review of Model Performance and Clinical Readiness
items.abstract: Leukaemia diagnosis and classification increasingly combine morphology with immunophenotypic, cytogenetic and molecular information, while artificial intelligence (AI) offers a potential means of standardising image-based assessment and reducing repetitive workload. This structured review critically examines contemporary AI approaches for leukaemia cell and case classification, with emphasis on dataset scale, unit of analysis, validation design, reported performance and clinical readiness. Peer-reviewed literature was identified through a targeted PubMed-focused search updated on 30 July 2026, with publisher and DOI records used to verify study design, numerical results and bibliographic identity. Representative primary human studies were selected only when the reported task, unit of analysis, testing design and principal performance metrics could be verified from the primary report. The evidence shows substantial technical progress, but the interpretation of apparently high performance changes markedly with the level at which generalisation is tested. Image-wise or closely related internal partitions provide weaker evidence of transportability than patient-level internal testing, while genuinely independent institutional or imaging-platform evaluation provides the most clinically informative test of robustness. Across acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, acute myeloid leukaemia and acute promyelocytic leukaemia applications, patient-level separation, external testing, class-balance reporting, transparent reference standards and multimodal diagnostic integration remain decisive. AI should therefore be considered an adjunct to expert haematopathology rather than a stand-alone substitute for contemporary integrated diagnosis. Multicentre prospective evaluation, rigorous reporting and clinically meaningful human-AI workflow studies are priorities for translation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Governance in Africa: Institutional Capacity, Regulation and Policy Implementation
items.abstract: In Africa, the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming part of the economic policy-making process, public administration, service delivery and technological development. Governments are preparing national AI strategies, creating institutional structures and joining in new continental and global governance efforts. The African Union's 2024 adoption of the Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy is an important milestone in the journey toward a coordinated African approach to AI governance (African Union [AU], 2024). But having a strategy or rules does not always mean it is implemented. This article explores the intersection of institutional capacity, regulation and policy implementation in the context of AI governance in Africa. The article presents the evidence from the recent African Union, OECD, UNESCO, World Bank and national AI institutions in Nigeria, and suggests that the reality of the problem is now more about implementation capacity than just about missing policies. African governments are constrained by complex challenges related to digital infrastructure, computing power, data management, technical skills, institutional coordination, finance and regulatory oversight. Infrastructure and compute challenges, lack of funding, and institutional coordination difficulties, as well as a shortage of AI-specific regulatory expertise, are all shared challenges across the countries (OECD, 2026). World Bank also states that connectivity, compute, data and skills are key prerequisites for meaningful AI adoption and governance (World Bank, 2025). The article concludes that the effective governance of AI in Africa demands to build the technical capacity of the public sector, create measurable mechanisms for implementation, foster inter-agency coordination, invest in building capacity to cooperate across the continent, and strengthen existing regulatory institutions. AI governance is thus more than a technology or regulatory matter; it is a governance challenge concerning state capacity and institutional effectiveness. In sum, this paper examines institutional capacity and regulation for AI governance in Africa, focusing on the specific issue of how to implement policy. This paper discusses institutional capacity and regulation for AI governance in Africa, particularly the question of the implementation of policy.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Use and Learner Autonomy Among Secondary Students: The Roles of AI Literacy and Metacognitive Self-Regulation
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in secondary education has created new opportunities for personalized support, immediate feedback, problem-solving, and self-directed learning, while also raising concerns about students’ reliance on AI-generated information. This narrative literature review examined AI use and learner autonomy among secondary students, with particular attention to the roles of AI literacy and metacognitive self-regulation. Recent literature published primarily from 2021 to 2026 was identified, screened, and synthesized through narrative and reflexive thematic analysis. Across the reviewed studies, AI supported learner autonomy most clearly when students used it for exploration, feedback, problem-solving, and self-regulated learning rather than as a substitute for independent thinking. AI literacy helped students understand AI, evaluate generated information, recognize its limitations, and make responsible decisions about its use. Metacognitive self-regulation, in turn, supported students in planning, monitoring, and evaluating their learning while working with AI. The literature also pointed to challenges, including excessive reliance on AI, limited AI knowledge, inconsistent learner engagement, and differences in self-regulatory abilities. Overall, learner autonomy in AI-supported settings depends on how students use the technology and on the development of AI literacy and metacognitive self-regulation with appropriate teacher guidance. The study contributes primarily to Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by supporting responsible and learner-centered integration of AI in secondary education. From a sustainability perspective, strengthening students’ critical and self-regulatory competencies may promote more responsible, adaptable, and sustainable use of emerging digital technologies in education.

items.title: Artificial intelligence use, creative thinking disposition, and metacognitive awareness among EFL learners: a structural equation modelling approach
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in English as a foreign language (EFL) learning, yet its cognitive implications depend on how learners engage with it rather than on its use alone. This study examined the structural relationships among differentiated patterns of AI use, creative thinking disposition, and metacognitive awareness among undergraduate EFL learners. Using a quantitative cross-sectional correlational design, data were collected from 713 learners and analysed through structural equation modelling. AI use was conceptualised as cognitive-support use, creative-extension use, reproductive or substitutive use, and ethical and critical awareness. The findings indicate that the use of cognitive-support and creative-extension AI is positively associated with both creative thinking disposition and metacognitive awareness. In contrast, reproductive or substitutive use is negatively associated with these outcomes. Creative thinking disposition demonstrates a strong positive relationship with metacognitive awareness and mediates the effects of constructive AI use on regulatory awareness. Ethical and critical engagement with AI moderates these relationships, strengthening the positive associations between constructive AI use and both creative and metacognitive outcomes. The results clarify that the cognitive value of AI in EFL learning is shaped by learner agency, reflective judgement, and responsibility for meaning-making. The study advances a cognitively grounded account of AI-mediated EFL learning and provides empirical support for differentiating AI engagement patterns in both research and instructional design.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Theranostics: Integrating Machine Learning For Precision Diagnosis And Personalized Therapy
items.abstract: Theranostics links disease characterization with treatment selection and response assessment, creating a framework in which diagnostic information directly informs individualized therapy. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), deep learning, radiomics, radiogenomics, and multimodal data integration are expanding this concept from target verification toward quantitative prediction of diagnosis, prognosis, therapeutic response, dose, and toxicity. This review examines how AI can connect imaging, electronic health records, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, pharmacogenomics, and treatment response data across a unified theranostic workflow. Evidence from ophthalmology, dermatology, pathology, cardiology, oncology, drug response prediction, radiopharmaceutical therapy, and personalized dosing demonstrates that ML models can extract clinically useful patterns from complex datasets and support patient level stratification. In nuclear medicine, AI assisted segmentation, quantitative imaging, and dosimetry may shorten analysis time and facilitate patient-specific radiopharmaceutical therapy. In precision oncology, radiomics and radiogenomics can associate imaging phenotypes with molecular characteristics and treatment outcomes, while computational drug response models can prioritize therapies for molecularly defined disease. However, clinical translation remains constrained by dataset shift, limited external validation, data leakage, class imbalance, algorithmic bias, interpretability, privacy, interoperability, regulatory uncertainty, and insufficient prospective evidence. Future progress will require multicenter datasets, standardized data pipelines, transparent reporting, calibrated uncertainty, explainable models, federated or privacy preserving learning, prospective clinical trials, and continuous post deployment monitoring. AI driven theranostics is therefore best viewed as a decision support ecosystem in which computational prediction complements, rather than replaces, clinical expertise and experimentally validated treatment pathways.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-enabled value creation and competitive advantage in marketing: A dynamic capabilities perspective
items.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities contribute to marketing value creation and competitive advantage by integrating customer data, marketing intelligence, operational execution, and human strategic oversight. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design combined a survey of 300 marketing executives with qualitative evidence from three digital-first brand cases to examine AI maturity, predictive analytics, marketing integration, automation, and performance outcomes. Organizations with higher AI maturity reported 25.4% lower customer acquisition costs (CAC) than those with lower AI maturity, while Generative AI (GenAI) users reported a 40% reduction in content-production time. Qualitative evidence indicates that predictive customer intelligence can enable more anticipatory and personalized engagement, while human oversight, data governance, and authenticity remain important boundary conditions. Synthetic data offers a complementary option for privacy-conscious experimentation and model development. The AI-Marketing Value Creation Model conceptualizes competitive advantage as the coordinated conversion of customer data and AI capabilities into economic, operational, and experiential value through organizational processes and human judgment. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Marketing Intelligence, Marketing Operations, Competitive Advantage, Dynamic Capabilities.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-enabled value creation and competitive advantage in supply chain management: A dynamic capabilities perspective
items.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) creates strategic value in supply chain management (SCM) by integrating technological capabilities, organizational agility, and human expertise. Using a mixed-methods design, the study combines quantitative survey data from 250 global supply chain executives with three qualitative industry case studies to develop the Artificial Intelligence–Supply Chain Management (AI-SCM) Value Creation Framework, grounded in Dynamic Capabilities Theory. Organizations with higher AI maturity reported 31.5% higher demand-forecast accuracy and 14.5% lower logistics and freight costs. Qualitative evidence indicates that AI-enabled predictive analytics, adaptive decision-making, and operational integration can strengthen supply chain agility and resilience. AI can function as an embedded strategic capability when supported by organizational readiness, reliable data, and human expertise. However, these benefits are not unconditional. Environmental burdens associated with AI infrastructure and algorithmic management risks, including surveillance and reduced worker autonomy, require responsible governance and meaningful human oversight. AI-enabled value creation is therefore contingent on technological capability, organizational conditions, and responsible human-AI integration. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Supply Chain Management, Competitive Advantage, Dynamic Capabilities, Value Creation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence; Rethinking- Learning in an Era of HumanMade Technology and Capitalist Mechanism
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) have revolutionised the interaction between humans, knowledge and technology. What once needed years of formal education, years of institutional access or specialist's help is now obtained, translated, explained, reorganised in seconds. This unprecedented accessibility can help to minimize some of the age disadvantages in learning and provide lifelong education. Meanwhile, it asks the essential question: With the ready availability of answers, and analyses the decisions through own judgement, curiosity, critical understanding and intellectual independence. This paper critically discusses the overlaps between AI, Age, Education, Automation and Capitalism. But it's not necessarily the democratisation of education, it says, arguing that the democratisation of access to AI shouldn't be equated with the democratisation of education. While it can overturn the notion that technological skills are predominantly the purview of younger people, the potential for age disparities leading compounded differences in access to these tools, algorithmic bias, and confidence gaps and differences in digital and AI literacy. At the same time, the increasing machine-like nature of the educational activities threatening to change the purpose of education from learning and human development to efficiency, productivity and measurable outcome is awaited niche. Literature-based analysis is carried out by reference to the UNESCO, OECD, Stanford AI Index, IMF, ILO, and peer-reviewed scholarship along with the theoretical approaches of critical pedagogy, digital ageism and technological capitalism. Based on secondary data, the use of AI by students is already prevalent and evidence about the impacts on learning is mixed, and largely dependent on the context of use. This paper suggests neither technological rejection nor unconditional adoption. Rather, a human-centred approach should be pursued where AI is a tool for intellectual work and not an intellectual replacement in education systems. AI literacy, critical thinking, intergenerational learning, teacher agency, and transparent assessment and equitable access, therefore, should be central to modern education.

items.title: Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can contribute to the reasoning and communication represented in student work, complicating inferences from product quality to individual capability. This conceptual article develops an integrated framework for assessing cognitive ownership through mutual evaluation and outcome-aligned verification. Cognitive ownership is defined as a learner’s demonstrated capacity to understand, evaluate, adapt, and accept responsibility for consequential reasoning under specified conditions of assistance. Eight indicators are organized into four assessment domains: understanding, epistemic judgment, adaptive performance, and reflective accountability. Mutual evaluation combines independent student and instructor judgments, evidence-based comparison, and documented responses to disagreement; agreement is not treated as proof of learning. The framework distinguishes the quality of an AI-assisted product, capability demonstrated during assessment, and learning established through change and retention. A worked higher education example illustrates task design, scoring, and responses to conflicting evidence. Five propositions and a validation agenda address incremental predictive value, task sampling, feedback, fairness, and feasibility. The framework is proposed rather than empirically validated. Its contribution is to connect existing validity and evaluative judgment scholarship with a practical account of the evidence needed to support bounded claims about individual and assisted performance.

items.title: Back to the Future: Regressing Readability Features from LLMs
items.abstract: Code readability supports software understanding, review, and maintenance. As AI coding agents become more widely used, readable code helps both humans review agent-generated output and agents maintain code within limited context windows. Yet existing readability models do not consistently agree with human judgements across datasets. We introduce BTTF (Back To The Future), pairing linear regression with information-theoretic features. Rather than using language models as black-box judges, BTTF uses them as measurement instruments. It combines traditional code measurements, embedding-based semantic organisation, and causal-LM predictability to capture source structure, semantic coherence, and contextual surprise. We evaluate BTTF on five publicly available human-rated readability benchmarks and our manually annotated MBJP development set, totalling 1,100 samples. BTTF improves average Spearman correlation over the strongest baseline by up to 0.101. Across 13 controlled readability-reducing transformations on production code, it achieves response rates of 93.8% in Java and 87.6% in Python, outperforming Dorn by 14% and 19.2%. It performs best among local models and trails the strongest cloud-LLM response by 1.7% in Java and 5.1% in Python. The direct-LLM baselines require an average of 1,083 prompt tokens per evaluation while remaining opaque. BTTF combines state-of-the-art benchmark performance and strong transformation robustness with feature-granular interpretability: every feature coefficient matches its theoretical directional effect across all evaluated model configurations.

items.title: Beyond AI Use: Examining The Predictive Quality of AI Dependency & Distress Intolerance in Avoidance Coping Among Young Adults in Mumbai
items.abstract: Abstract Background: As the reliance on AI keeps growing, it becomes important to understand its psychological implications. The study contributes to the growing literature on AI and mental health by investigating the predictive quality of AI dependency and distress tolerance in the use of avoidance coping in response to stressful situations. Aims: The present research aims to examine the predictive relationship between AI dependency, distress intolerance and avoidance coping among young adults in Mumbai. Method: 90 participants from Mumbai (60 Females, 29 Males) who were aged between 18-25 years (M=20.8, SD=2.38) and used AI apps like ChatGPT and Gemini, were selected using convenience sampling. All participants completed the Generative AI Dependency Scale (Goh et al., 2025), Distress Tolerance Scale (Simons & Gaher, 2005) and Ways of Coping Scale-Revised (Folkman & Lazarus, 1985). Correlation and simple linear regression was computed for statistical analysis. Results: Findings of the research indicate that AI dependency showed a significant positive correlation with avoidance coping (p < .01) and hence was a statistically significant predictor. Furthermore, distress intolerance showed a weak correlation with avoidance coping and was therefore not a statistically significant predictor (p > .05) of avoidance coping. Conclusion: The findings of this study highlight the predictive role of AI dependency in the use of avoidance coping when faced with stressful situations. The role of distress tolerance in avoidance coping needs to be studied further in a more diverse and larger population. The findings may help develop strategies that promote healthy coping skills in stressful situations in the era of increasing AI use.

items.title: Bridging the Human-AI preference gap: A persuasion-oriented tripartite framework
items.abstract: The remarkable performance of artificial intelligence (AI) systems on a wide variety of complex tasks has fueled its rapid adoption in recent years. Yet, many individuals still exhibit a human-AI preference gap, such that they prefer human-generated over AI-generated outputs and follow recommendations made by generative AI (GenAI) less than human advice. We conceptualize the rejection of a superior AI system in favor of an inferior human as a persuasion failure that necessitates psychological rather than technological resolution. Recent research has identified various interventions that compress the human-AI preference gap. We codify these interventions by introducing a persuasion-oriented tripartite framework that delineates three distinct paths by which the preference gap between humans and AI systems may be narrowed: (1) AI-centric interventions, which directly bolster perceptions and evaluations of AI systems; (2) human-centric interventions, which reduce the (often inflated) perceptions and evaluations of humans; and (3) hybrid interventions, which offer an integrated or reformulated alternative that combines human and AI elements. Ultimately, our tripartite framework illustrates how different persuasion tactics fundamentally reshape beliefs and attitudes about both AI and humans, thereby informing system design elements and communication strategies that can bridge the human-AI preference gap.

items.title: ChatGPT Use and Learning Motivation among Informatics Students: A Preliminary Correlational Study
items.abstract: Generative AI systems such as ChatGPT are increasingly used by university students for explanation, code inspection, idea generation, and immediate feedback. This preliminary cross-sectional study examines the association between ChatGPT use frequency and learning motivation among 17 Informatics Engineering students at Universitas Mulia, Balikpapan. Data were collected through an online questionnaire using a four-category measure of ChatGPT use frequency and four-point agreement responses for learning motivation. The original analysis reported a Pearson correlation of r = 0.685 with p = 0.002. Using the reported coefficient and sample size, the corresponding test statistic is t(15) = 3.642 and the Fisher-transformed 95% confidence interval is approximately 0.305-0.877, indicating a positive but imprecisely estimated association. The finding is consistent with literature suggesting that responsive AI tools may support engagement and perceived competence, but the correlational design does not establish that ChatGPT use increases motivation. Reverse causality, self-selection, prior achievement, digital confidence, purpose of use, and measurement limitations remain plausible explanations. The study contributes context-specific evidence from informatics students and identifies requirements for stronger follow-up research, including a larger sample, validated motivation measures, clearer characterization of AI use, rank-based sensitivity analysis, and longitudinal or quasi-experimental data.

items.title: Comparing artificial intelligence versus human screening in systematic reviews
items.abstract: Systematic reviews are essential for informing health policy and practice. Artificial intelligence (AI) automates the article screening process and produces time savings, although the performance of AI screening compared to traditional human screening remains uncertain. We undertook this study to compare the performance of two agentic AI tools, namely Loon Lens TM and Catchii, to one another and to humans at the title and abstract screening level. We also compared Loon Lens to humans at the full-text screening level. We developed a de novo research question on the association between any of three ambient air pollutants – carbon monoxide, ozone, nitrogen dioxide – and the onset or worsening of Parkinson’s disease. A health sciences librarian developed the literature search strategy and we proceeded with human and AI screening. Screening results were compared using sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, concordance, kappa, and F1 score. We contrasted these statistics to those obtained by naïve guessing and regressed concordance (agree or disagree with the human reference standard) onto confidence scores provided by Loon Lens, which assigned a confidence level (‘Very High’, ‘High’, Medium’, or ‘Low’) to each of its screening decisions. Human screening was the reference standard against both AI tools; Catchii was the reference standard against Loon Lens. At title and abstract screening, Loon Lens outperformed Catchii when humans were the reference standard (Loon Lens versus human: sensitivity = 0.66, kappa = 0.74, F1 = 0.76; Catchii versus human: sensitivity = 0.49, kappa = 0.46, F1 = 0.50). At full-text screening, most disagreements centered around articles Loon Lens included and humans excluded. At both screening levels, higher confidence scores were associated with lower odds of disagreement between Loon Lens and human screeners. Given the panoply of available AI screening tools and their differential performance, plus the rapidly evolving nature of AI technology, researchers should pilot test their chosen tool at the start of each review. Sensitivity, kappa, and F1 are the optimal performance statistics to employ, especially at title and abstract screening, where the imbalance between proportions of included and excluded citations can inflate concordance and negative predictive value.
